title: The kitchen at Amritsar
hook: the langar at the Golden Temple feeds tens of thousands every day

segments.voice: Yesterday, planting forests, and your line was a forest for nanak. Did you plant or water something? Today, from the forest to a kitchen in Amritsar. Day one thousand forty-three.

The sound comes first. Steel plates, stacked and passed and clattering, a rolling metal river of them. Then the smell: lentils, butter, fresh roti. Then the hall itself, at the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, also called the Golden Temple. People sit on long strips of matting on the floor, row after row: a farmer, a tourist with a camera around her neck, a businessman, a grandmother, a child. A volunteer walks down the row with a bucket of dal, ladling it onto every plate in the same amount. Nobody asks who you are. Today, the kitchen at Amritsar.
screen: `A RIVER OF STEEL PLATES.` → `ROW AFTER ROW ON THE FLOOR.` → `NOBODY ASKS WHO YOU ARE.`

segments.voice: First, the size. The gurdwara's own accounts say its langar feeds tens of thousands of people every day, and more on festival days. The food is free. Volunteers do much of the work: kneading dough, rolling roti, stirring huge pots, washing plates. Second, the rows. The sitting in rows is called pangat. Everyone eats at the same level, the same food, from the same kitchen. There is no head table, and no better plate for an important guest. Third, the emperor on the floor. Tradition tells that when the emperor Akbar came to meet Guru Amar Das, he was asked to do what everyone did first: sit in the pangat and eat langar. Sikhs sum up the old rule in a short phrase: pehle pangat, piche sangat. First the row, then the gathering. A ruler of an empire, the story goes, sat on the floor beside whoever was there. Fourth, the plates. After the meal comes the washing. Visitors line up to scrub steel next to students and farmers. The hands get wrinkled, the plates go back out, and the river keeps flowing. That's today's line: tens of thousands fed. Not a statistic. A meal, multiplied, and every plate given the same.
screen: `FREE FOOD, CARRIED BY VOLUNTEERS.` · `PANGAT: EVERYONE IN THE SAME ROW.` · `FIRST THE ROW, THEN THE GATHERING.` · `WASHING THE PLATES.` · then, large: `TENS OF THOUSANDS FED.`

segments.voice: Two minutes in the rows. Sit, and let your breath slow. Picture the hall: the long mats, the people sitting side by side, the volunteer coming down the line with a bucket. Put yourself in the row. Who's on your left? A stranger. On your right? Another. Now see the plate land in front of you, the same as theirs. Breathe in, receiving. Breathe out, and picture yourself up at the sinks, washing someone else's plate. If you pray, you can say Waheguru on each breath out. The bell holds the time.
Pangat. The row where everyone sits together to eat, at the Harmandir Sahib's langar in Amritsar, with free meals served to everyone who comes. Today's word.

Your line: tens of thousands fed. That ends a week of Sikh life now: help out of addiction, a turban chosen, the word on screens, honest pictures, a clean river, a forest, and this kitchen. Today, at one meal, serve someone else first, or wash a plate that isn't yours. Day one thousand forty-three.

howItsDone: At the Harmandir Sahib in Amritsar, the langar serves free vegetarian meals to all visitors, who sit together in rows (pangat) on the floor; volunteers cook, serve and wash the dishes as seva.
